summary: Describes EAP-pwd, an Extensible Authentication Protocol method that authenticates with a shared password, even a weak one an attacker could guess from a dictionary. The key exchange resists active, passive and dictionary attacks. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Prove you know a password without ever saying it, so an eavesdropper cannot figure it out even if the password is easy.

questions: how does eap-pwd resist dictionary attacks
what is the eap-pwd method type
subtitle: A way to log in to a network with just a password, even a guessable one, without handing an eavesdropper anything to crack offline.

tldr.problem: People typically authenticate with passwords that are easy to type and therefore weak, and an attacker with a dictionary could guess them if a protocol exposed anything to test guesses against.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-pwd runs a password-authenticated key exchange in three exchanges (ID, Commit, Confirm). Each side derives a Password Element from the password and mixes in secret random numbers, so each protocol run lets an attacker test at most one password guess.
tldr.outcome: The key exchange is designed to resist passive, active and dictionary attack and to provide forward secrecy, and it produces a 512-bit MSK and EMSK. It does not stop repeated online guessing, so implementations are told to use a large dictionary and lock out repeated failures. It is informational and is updated by RFC 8146.

today: RFC 5931 is an Informational RFC and is updated by RFC 8146. It has not been obsoleted, so the two are read together. The RFC defines the EAP-pwd method and leaves online guessing limits to implementations.

sections.title: Passwords and Weak Secrets
sections.content:
The usual way into the Internet is a person typing a username and password. Because people must enter these repeatedly without errors, the passwords are likely low-entropy, and the RFC assumes an adversary with a dictionary can guess them. EAP-pwd is an Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) method for this problem, known as password-based authenticated key exchange: use a possibly weak password to derive an authenticated, cryptographically strong shared secret.

The RFC states that such a protocol must be resistant to passive attack, active attack and dictionary attack, and must have forward secrecy. In a dictionary attack, any advantage the adversary gets must come from interactions with an honest party, not from computation, so she can learn only whether a single guess from a single run is right.
sections.eli5: Easy-to-remember passwords are easy to guess. This protocol makes sure a guesser only gets one try each time they bother the real server.

sections.title: Groups, Hashes and the Password Element
sections.content:
EAP-pwd does its math in a cryptographic group, built either from finite field cryptography (FFC) or elliptic curve cryptography (ECC). Only ECC groups over GF(p) with a co-factor of one are allowed; groups over GF(2^m) SHALL NOT be used. A Ciphersuite bundles the group, a random function H and a pseudo-random function (PRF). H is HMAC-SHA256 with a 32-octet key of zeros, and the key derivation function follows the counter-mode-with-feedback construction from the NIST recommendation it cites.

Both sides turn the password into a Password Element (PWE) in the group by a loop the RFC calls hunting and pecking. It hashes a token, both identities, the password and a counter, expands the result, and tries to use it as a point or group element, incrementing the counter until it works. To an attacker without the password, the result looks like a random group element. Before this step the password is pre-processed in one of three ways: none, as defined in RFC 2759, or SASLprep.
sections.eli5: Both of you use the secret word to pick the same special point on a big map. Nobody else can tell which point it is, because it looks random to them.

sections.title: The Three Exchanges
sections.content:
An EAP-pwd run has three exchanges. In the ID exchange the server sends its identity, a Ciphersuite, an anti-clogging token and the password pre-processing method, and the peer acknowledges them and adds its own identity. The token is unpredictable and shows the peer is live rather than part of a flooding attack. If the peer does not accept the Ciphersuite or pre-processing method it answers with an EAP-NAK.

In the Commit exchange each side picks two random numbers, a secret and a mask. It sends a Scalar (their sum modulo the group order) and an Element computed from the mask and the Password Element. Receivers validate lengths, ranges and elements, and the server rejects a reflected copy of its own values. Each side then computes a shared value from its own secret and what it received.

In the Confirm exchange each side sends a hash binding that shared value, both Elements and Scalars, and the Ciphersuite. A mismatch ends the exchange, and a correct Confirm_P lets the server send EAP-Success. The master key is MK = H(shared value | Confirm_P | Confirm_S).
sections.eli5: First you introduce yourselves, then you swap scrambled numbers, then you each show a stamp that only works if you both used the same secret word.

sections.title: Packet Formats and Fragmentation
sections.content:
EAP-pwd packets use a header with Code (1 for Request, 2 for Response), Identifier, Length, Type (52), then an L bit, an M bit and a 6-bit PWD-Exch field that says which exchange the payload belongs to, and an optional Total-Length. The ID payload carries a Group Description from the IKE registry, a Random Function, a PRF, the Token, a Prep byte for password pre-processing and the identity. Commit carries an Element and a Scalar; Confirm carries one hash value.

Group elements and scalars are fixed-width unsigned integers. An ECC element is the x-coordinate followed by the y-coordinate, so no compressed form is used. Because messages can exceed what EAP allows, EAP-pwd supports fragmentation. The L bit marks the first fragment and the M bit marks all but the last. The receiver acknowledges each fragment with an empty EAP-pwd message. The fragmentation threshold must be 1020 bytes unless the lower layer's MTU is known.
sections.eli5: If a letter is too long for one envelope, you split it across several. Each piece is marked so the other side knows more is coming and says 'got it' after each.

sections.title: Exported Keys
sections.content:
Following the advice in RFC 5247, EAP-pwd defines a Method-ID, H(Ciphersuite | Scalar_P | Scalar_S), and a Session-ID made of the Type code 52 followed by the Method-ID. The master key MK is stretched with the key derivation function into 1024 bits, split into a 512-bit MSK and a 512-bit EMSK. Keys are given names built from the Session-ID plus the letters of MSK or EMSK so key caching can find them.

For interoperability, implementations must support Diffie-Hellman group 19 from RFC 5114, the random function from the RFC, PRF HMAC-SHA256 and no password pre-processing.
sections.eli5: When the handshake is done, the shared secret is stretched into two longer keys, each given a label so they are easy to find later.

sections.title: How Well the Goals Are Met
sections.content:
A passive attacker sees the Scalars and Elements but does not know the secret random numbers, which are hidden by adding masks, so cannot compute MK. An active attacker who forges Commit messages is reduced to a passive one or cannot compute the shared value without the password. The RFC argues that the best an active attacker gains in one attempt is to learn whether one password guess was right, which is the definition of resistance to dictionary attack. Forward secrecy holds because fresh random values are chosen on every run, so learning the password later reveals nothing about earlier sessions.

There is a clear limit. An attacker can still make repeated online guesses, and the chance of success grows as failed guesses are removed from the pool. Implementations SHOULD make the dictionary size sufficiently large and SHOULD take countermeasures such as refusing attempts for a time after a threshold of failures; the RFC recommends no specific threshold or time. The mandatory group 19 uses a 256-bit prime and is estimated to give a 128-bit symmetric key.
sections.eli5: A cheater can still try guessing again and again at the front door, so the server should slow them down and passwords should not be too simple.
